articles.title: Research Dashboard Retrieval Architecture for Semantic Pagination Under Alert Pressure
articles.excerpt: Short answer: use a snapshot-bound cursor over a two-stage semantic search, and attach the snapshot ID to every page. That keeps a financial research dashboard from showing the same near-duplicate fil…
articles.body: Short answer: use a snapshot-bound cursor over a two-stage semantic search, and attach the snapshot ID to every page. That keeps a financial research dashboard from showing the same near-duplicate filing twice while an index refresh is running. The extra metadata costs a little latency; the alternative is an analyst chasing evidence that moved between pages. The page that wakes me up is usually not “search is down.” It is an analyst reporting that page two contains a duplicate of page one, or that a filing visible ten minutes ago vanished when they clicked Next. In a fintech dashboard, those are evidence defects. A green 200 response does not make them harmless. I work backwards from that alert.

articles.title: Support Retrieval Architecture: Node.js Traces Beat Log-Only Observability
articles.excerpt: Short answer: use trace-centered observability for a customer-support retrieval architecture, with structured events and freshness metrics attached to each trace. A log-only design is quick to ship, b…
articles.body: Short answer: use trace-centered observability for a customer-support retrieval architecture, with structured events and freshness metrics attached to each trace. A log-only design is quick to ship, but it makes a bad answer hard to explain because chunking, embedding, filtering, and reranking happen in different places. I build the ingestion path first: split support articles, attach stable metadata, embed the chunks, and write them to a vector index. The retrieval path then turns a ticket into candidate chunks for the language model. The important decision is not which dashboard looks nicest. It is whether one support answer can be reconstructed from source revision to final context.

articles.excerpt: The gap is not data, it is join keys Japan publishes more company data than most markets. EDINET has annual reports going back a decade, TDnet pushes earnings releases in near real time, JPX publishes…
articles.body: The gap is not data, it is join keys Japan publishes more company data than most markets. EDINET has annual reports going back a decade, TDnet pushes earnings releases in near real time, JPX publishes listing files, and none of it costs money. If you are writing English documentation for an agent that needs Japanese financials, the problem is not supply. The problem is that every one of those sources identifies a company differently, and the mismatch shows up at the join, not at the download. I spent the last months building a data pipeline over these sources and then a tool layer on top of it. Here is what I measured on the way, and which route I ended up keeping. Route one: EDINET, official and free EDINET is the Financial Services Agency's disclosure system.

articles.title: Queue Based Scheduled Database Cleanup for Large Datasets Explained
articles.excerpt: A large PostgreSQL cleanup can outlive a request, so the scheduler must not own the delete loop. Short answer: let cron start a job, split that job into deterministic queue messages, and let workers d…
articles.body: A large PostgreSQL cleanup can outlive a request, so the scheduler must not own the delete loop. Short answer: let cron start a job, split that job into deterministic queue messages, and let workers delete bounded chunks. For a nightly payment-provider reconciliation, this design trades a little queue latency for retry isolation, controlled database load, and a vendor boundary that can be replaced. Keep the messages small. Keep the identities stable. A queue delivery is a command to reconcile one tenant, table, or time range, not a container for the rows themselves. How should cron run scheduled database cleanup for a large dataset? The scheduler knows when work begins; it should not decide how thousands or millions of rows finish.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 19, 2005: Japan's Hayabusa spacecraft makes 1st-ever liftoff from surface of an asteroid
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Hayabusa was supposed to return asteroid samples to Earth. Asteroids are space rocks that were formed during the early solar system. We study asteroids to learn more about the solar system's history. Hayabusa (pronounced HI-uh-BOOS-uh) made two touchdowns on asteroid Itokawa (EE -toh-KA-wah). Each time, the spacecraft went into safe mode. Controllers weren't sure if Hayabusa gathered any material. But they sent the spacecraft back to Earth anyway. Hayabusa's sample return capsule returned to Earth in June 2010 . Scientists found dust of Itokawa inside the capsule, proving that it did indeed capture samples of Itokawa.

articles.title: No more asteroid landing: Engine trouble forces Japan's Hayabusa2 probe to change plans
articles.excerpt: Japan's space agency has decided to switch destinations and objectives for the final act of its Hayabusa2 asteroid mission, due to problems with the spacecraft's ion thrusters.
articles.body: Japan's space agency has decided to switch destinations and objectives for the final act of its Hayabusa2 mission, due to the spacecraft suffering trouble with its ion thrusters. The veteran Hayabusa2 spacecraft launched back in 2014 to collect material from the asteroid Ryugu . Since delivering the samples to Earth in December 2020 via a reentry capsule, the main spacecraft has been conducting an extended mission of exploration and in July made a super-close flyby of the two-headed asteroid Torifune. But Hayabusa2's continued adventures are now set for a premature end.

articles.title: China rolls out rocket for launch of 1st international astronaut to Tiangong space station (video)
articles.excerpt: China has rolled to the launch pad the rocket and spacecraft for its Shenzhou-24 mission, which will fly the first international astronaut to the nation's Tiangong space station.
articles.body: China's space station is set to receive its first foreign astronaut. A Long March 2F rocket, topped with the Shenzhou-24 crew spacecraft, was rolled out to the pad at Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China, on Tuesday (Nov. 17), with launch expected in the next week. The 191-foot-tall (58 meters) rocket was transferred 0.93 miles (1.5 kilometers) from a vertical integration building to the pad over the course of around two hours, starting around 4 a.m. EST (0900 GMT, or 5 p.m. Beijing Time), according to China Central Television (CCTV). China rolls out the Long March 2F rocket for its Shenzhou-24 astronaut mission on Nov. 17, 2026.
